arXiv:2510.22219v1 [cs.CL] 25 Oct 2025

Estimating the Error of Large Language Models at
Pairwise Text Comparison

Tianyi Li ††thanks: tianyi.li@cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: Department of Decisions, Operations and Technology, CUHK
Abstract

We measure LLMs’ output error at pairwise text comparison, noting the probability of error in their preferences. Our method does not rely on the ground truth and supports two scenarios: (i) uniform error rate regardless of the order of comparison, estimated with two comparisons for each text pair with either text placed first; (ii) binary positional bias assuming distinct error rates for the two orders of comparison, estimated with repeated comparisons between the texts. The Copeland counting constructs a ranking over the compared texts from pairwise preferences; the ranking reveals the poor scalability of LLM-based pairwise comparison and helps yield the estimates for LLMs’ error rates. We apply the method to six LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Qwen) with five types of text input and obtain consistent estimates of LLMs’ error. In general, the measured two positional bias terms are similar, close to the uniform error. Considering both the error rates and the robustness to the variation of prompts, Claude obtained the most desirable performance in this experiment. Our model outperforms the biased Bradley-Terry model and the commutativity score in indicating LLMs’ error at this task.

Hallucination (Ji et al., 2023; Chelli et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025), which leads to deceptive behavior (Hagendorff, 2024), is a rooted problem for the output from LLMs, where factual errors (Augenstein et al., 2024) contaminate the output due to generative models’ stochastic nature. The level of hallucination can be quantified by comparing the LLM output to the ground truth (Shen et al., 2023, e.g.,). When the ground truth is not available (Wei et al., 2024, e.g.,), particular settings could be conceived to help reveal LLMs’ errors. For example, ask the LLM the same question multiple times and see if the answers are consistent (Manakul et al., 2023, e.g.,).

The output’s consistency can be evaluated in a rigorous way when the answers are indicative rather than descriptive. A good setting in this regard is to use the LLM to compare input objects and ask it to output a preference. The delivered instances of preference from an ensemble of inquiries then help quantify the LLM output’s rate of error. Further, based on the results of comparison, a ranking over the compared objects can be constructed, which can be contrasted with the ground-truth ranking if there exists one (Liu et al., 2024b, e.g.,).

The basic format for this task is pairwise text comparison (Chen et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a, e.g.,), applicable to LLMs of different types and performance levels while extensible to, for example, setwise comparison (Zhuang et al., 2024) and other types of input such as at multimodel LLMs (Koh et al., 2023, e.g.,). A key aspect of evaluating LLMs’ output error via pairwise comparison is to swap the order of comparison and check the consistency of the two preferences, which is often violated – the indication of preference (i.e., object 1 or 2) remains unchanged when the comparison order is swapped. The hallucination of the LLM output exhibits here as order inconsistency (Zeng et al., 2024), sometimes termed as positional bias (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023): LLMs’ propensity to favor certain positional configurations of the input over others. As noted in (Zheng et al., 2023), positional bias at texts is prevalent in human decision-making (Blunch, 1984) and other machine-learning decision settings, e.g., learning-to-rank from click data (Wang et al., 2018) or question-answering models (Ko et al., 2020). It is important to study such a fallacy in this new context of human-machine exchange (Peter et al., 2025).

Another issue with employing LLMs in pairwise comparison is its poor scalability: the number of comparisons grows quadratically as the number of objects increases (Zheng et al., 2023; Liusie et al., 2024), and thus constructing a ranking from comparison results requires sub-sampling and algorithmic caveats to speed up (Qin et al., 2023, e.g.,). Besides the difficulty in computation, one can imagine that the reliability of objects’ ranking based on pairwise comparison also deteriorates when it scales up. It is useful to validate this conjecture with formal constructs.

In this work, we propose a method to characterize LLMs’ error-prone output when recruiting them for pairwise text comparison. The method captures the probability of error in the LLM-output preferences, considering two scenarios: (i) a uniform error rate regardless of the order of comparison, estimated with two comparisons for each text pair with either text placed first; (ii) the positional bias which assumes distinct error rates for the two orders of comparison, estimated with multiple instances of preference collected from a series of comparisons between the two objects. The classic Copeland counting (Copeland, 1951; Shah and Wainwright, 2018) is applied to construct a ranking over the compared objects from pairwise preferences. The obtained Copeland ranking demonstrates the poor scalability of LLM-based pairwise comparison and helps yield the estimates for LLMs’ error rates in this ground-truth-free setting. We apply the method to data obtained from six popular LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Qwen) with five types of text input (pseudo-word paragraphs, pseudo paragraphs, advertising slogans, short poems, academic abstracts); results yield consistent estimates of LLMs’ error across the two scenarios. Our estimates align with the commutativity scores (Liu et al., 2024a) while indicating LLMs’ error to a better extent. We construct a biased Bradley-Terry (BT) model (Bradley and Terry, 1952) for alternative error estimation; our model outperforms the biased BT model in delivering coherent estimates.

Methods

Consider an ensemble of NN texts. Suppose the ground-truth outcome of comparing text ii to text jj is yi​j∈[−1,1]y_{ij}\in[-1,1], and the LLM-output preference is y^i​j∈[−1,1]\hat{y}_{ij}\in[-1,1]; for both, -1/1 means text ii is not preferred/preferred to jj. When swapping the order of comparison, the ground-truth/LLM-output preference is yj​iy_{ji} and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji}, respectively. For the ground truth, yi​j=−yj​iy_{ij}=-y_{ji}, while it is likely that y^i​j=y^j​i\hat{y}_{ij}=\hat{y}_{ji}, as the LLM output may contain error. Denote the matrices 𝐘𝐠={yi​j}\mathbf{Y_{g}}=\{y_{ij}\} and 𝐘={y^i​j}\mathbf{Y}=\{\hat{y}_{ij}\}. The commutativity (Ramík, 2020, e.g.,) score Sc​o​m∈[0,1]S_{com}\in[0,1] proposed in (Liu et al., 2024a) evaluates the proportion of comparisons having the opposite preference when the comparison order is swapped, i.e., the proportion of cases demonstrating inconsistent output across the two instances of comparison. It can be calculated from the matrix 𝐘\mathbf{Y}: Sc​o​m=2/N(N−1)∑i<j𝟙[y^i​j=y^j​i]S_{com}=2/N(N-1)\sum_{i<j}\mathbbm{1}[\hat{y}_{ij}=\hat{y}_{ji}]. A small/large Sc​o​mS_{com} indicates a small/large error rate over the ensemble of comparisons.

Uniform error

Suppose that the LLM-output preference y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} contains error with probability ϵ\epsilon, uniformly for any i,ji,j:

∀i,j,y^i​j={yi​j​ [True],P=1−ϵ,−yi​j​ [False],P=ϵ.\forall i,j,\ \ \ \hat{y}_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{ij}\text{ [True]},\ \ P=1-\epsilon,\\ -&y_{ij}\text{ [False]},\ \ P=\epsilon.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (1)

Averaging the outcomes y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji} from the two instances of comparison between ii and jj, we obtain

z^i​j=y^i​j+(−y^j​i)2,\hat{z}_{ij}=\frac{\hat{y}_{ij}+(-\hat{y}_{ji})}{2}, (2)

which constitutes the matrix 𝐙={z^i​j}\mathbf{Z}=\{\hat{z}_{ij}\}. 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is diagonally antisymmetric: z^i​j=−z^j​i\hat{z}_{ij}=-\hat{z}_{ji}. There are four cases for the outcome at z^i​j\hat{z}_{ij}: (i) when y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} is False and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji} is True, z^i​j=0\hat{z}_{ij}=0; (ii) when y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} is True and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji} is True, z^i​j=yi​j\hat{z}_{ij}=y_{ij}; (iii) when y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} is False and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji} is False, z^i​j=−yi​j\hat{z}_{ij}=-y_{ij}; (iv) when y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} is True and y^j​i\hat{y}_{ji} is False, z^i​j=0\hat{z}_{ij}=0. Cases (i) and (iv) yield the same outcome; the probabilities for different values of z^i​j\hat{z}_{ij} are

{P⁡(z^i​j=0)=2​ϵ​(1−ϵ),P⁡(z^i​j=yi​j​[True outcome (TO)])=(1−ϵ)2,P⁡(z^i​j=−yi​j​[Inverse outcome (IO)])=ϵ2.\left\{\begin{aligned} &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=0)&&=2\epsilon(1-\epsilon),\\ &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=y_{ij}\ \text{[True outcome (TO)]})&&=(1-\epsilon)^{2},\\ &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=-y_{ij}\ \text{[Inverse outcome (IO)]})&&=\epsilon^{2}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (3)

We use the Copeland counting to construct a ranking of the texts. The Copeland ranking relies on the scores that sum on the matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z}: the score for text ii is

SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZ​(i)=∑jN−1z^i​j,S_{Copeland}^{Z}(i)=\sum_{j}^{N-1}\hat{z}_{ij}, (4)

Positional bias

The positional bias considers that the error rates are different when the text is in the first or second place of the comparison: when the better text is placed first/second, the error rate is ϵ+/ϵ−\epsilon_{+}/\epsilon_{-}. This extends the uniform error probability to:

yi​j=1,\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ y_{ij}=1, y^i​j={yi​j​ [True],P=1−ϵ+,−yi​j​ [False],P=ϵ+. andy^j​i={yj​i​ [True],P=1−ϵ−,−yj​i​ [False],P=ϵ−.\displaystyle\hat{y}_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{ij}\text{ [True]},\ \ P=1-\epsilon_{+},\\ -&y_{ij}\text{ [False]},\ \ P=\epsilon_{+}.\\ \end{aligned}\right.\text{ and}\ \ \ \hat{y}_{ji}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{ji}\text{ [True]},\ \ P=1-\epsilon_{-},\\ -&y_{ji}\text{ [False]},\ \ P=\epsilon_{-}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (14)
yi​j=−1,\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ y_{ij}=-1, y^i​j={yi​j​ [True],P=1−ϵ−,−yi​j​ [False],P=ϵ−. andy^j​i={yj​i​ [True],P=1−ϵ+,−yj​i​ [False],P=ϵ+.\displaystyle\hat{y}_{ij}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{ij}\text{ [True]},\ \ P=1-\epsilon_{-},\\ -&y_{ij}\text{ [False]},\ \ P=\epsilon_{-}.\\ \end{aligned}\right.\text{ and}\ \ \ \hat{y}_{ji}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{ji}\text{ [True]},\ \ P=1-\epsilon_{+},\\ -&y_{ji}\text{ [False]},\ \ P=\epsilon_{+}.\\ \end{aligned}\right.

The probabilities for different values of z^i​j\hat{z}_{ij} are now

{P⁡(z^i​j=0)=ϵ+​(1−ϵ−)+ϵ−​(1−ϵ+),P⁡(z^i​j=yi​j​[True outcome (TO)])=(1−ϵ+)​(1−ϵ−),P⁡(z^i​j=−yi​j​[Inverse outcome (IO)])=ϵ+​ϵ−.\left\{\begin{aligned} &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=0)&&=\epsilon_{+}(1-\epsilon_{-})+\epsilon_{-}(1-\epsilon_{+}),\\ &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=y_{ij}\ \text{[True outcome (TO)]})&&=(1-\epsilon_{+})(1-\epsilon_{-}),\\ &P(\hat{z}_{ij}=-y_{ij}\ \text{[Inverse outcome (IO)]})&&=\epsilon_{+}\epsilon_{-}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (15)

with the second half m>(N+1)/2m>(N+1)/2 mirroring the first half m≤(N+1)/2m\leq(N+1)/2 via the substitution m−1→N−mm-1\rightarrow N-m.

This formulation nonetheless does not separate ϵ+\epsilon_{+} and ϵ−\epsilon_{-}, which always appear together in (1−ϵ+)​(1−ϵ−)(1-\epsilon_{+})(1-\epsilon_{-}) or ϵ+​ϵ−\epsilon_{+}\epsilon_{-}. To separate the two error terms for possible estimation, we can conduct repeated comparisons between each pair of objects.

Consider repeated comparisons between ii and jj in a series of instances denoted by KK (e.g., K=[+,−,+,−,…]K=[+,-,+,-,...]) in which there are k+k_{+} instances of ++, i.e., object ii is in the first place and the outcome is y^i​j,t\hat{y}_{ij,t} (the tt-th such case), and k−k_{-} instances of −-, i.e., object jj is in the first place and the outcome is y^j​i,t\hat{y}_{ji,t} (the tt-th such case). Consider separate error terms ϵ+\epsilon_{+}, ϵ−\epsilon_{-}. Define the observation matrix 𝐖={w^i​j}\mathbf{W}=\{\hat{w}_{ij}\} (antisymmetric, w^i​j=−w^j​i\hat{w}_{ij}=-\hat{w}_{ji}), where

w^i​j=w^i​j​(K)≈w^i​j​(k+,k−)=∑k+y^i​j,∙−∑k−y^j​i,∙k++k−.\hat{w}_{ij}=\hat{w}_{ij}(K)\approx\hat{w}_{ij}(k_{+},k_{-})=\frac{\sum^{k_{+}}\hat{y}_{ij,\bullet}-\sum^{k_{-}}\hat{y}_{ji,\bullet}}{k_{+}+k_{-}}. (17)

This assumes that the sequence of KK breaks down to the two counts k+k_{+} and k−k_{-}. The two sums in the numerator are taken over the two categories of outcomes, respectively. 𝐖={w^i​j}\mathbf{W}=\{\hat{w}_{ij}\} reduces to 𝐙={z^i​j}\mathbf{Z}=\{\hat{z}_{ij}\} when k+=k−=1k_{+}=k_{-}=1.

Unlike at the uniform error, where there are only three possible values (1, 0, -1) for z^i​j\hat{z}_{ij}, now there are 1+k++k−1+k_{+}+k_{-} possible values for w^i​j\hat{w}_{ij}: 1,k++k−−2k++k−,k++k−−4k++k−,k++k−−6k++k−,…,−11,\frac{k_{+}+k_{-}-2}{k_{+}+k_{-}},\frac{k_{+}+k_{-}-4}{k_{+}+k_{-}},\frac{k_{+}+k_{-}-6}{k_{+}+k_{-}},...,-1. The probabilities for observing these values at w^i​j\hat{w}_{ij} are given by (suppose the ground truth yi​j=1y_{ij}=1)

P⁡(w^i​j=k++k−−2​mk++k−)=∑m+∈[0,k+];m−∈[0,k−]m++m−=mCk+m+​Ck−m−​(1−ϵ+)k+−m+​(1−ϵ−)k−−m−​ϵ+m+​ϵ−m−;P(\hat{w}_{ij}=\frac{k_{+}+k_{-}-2m}{k_{+}+k_{-}})=\sum^{m_{+}+m_{-}=m}_{m_{+}\in[0,k_{+}];m_{-}\in[0,k_{-}]}C_{k_{+}}^{m_{+}}C_{k_{-}}^{m_{-}}(1-\epsilon_{+})^{k_{+}-m_{+}}(1-\epsilon_{-})^{k_{-}-m_{-}}\epsilon_{+}^{m_{+}}\epsilon_{-}^{m_{-}}; (18)

in particular,

{P⁡(w^i​j=yi​j​[True outcome (TO)])=(1−ϵ+)k+​(1−ϵ−)k−,P⁡(w^i​j=−yi​j​[Inverse outcome (IO)])=ϵ+k+​ϵ−k−.\left\{\begin{aligned} &P(\hat{w}_{ij}=y_{ij}\ \text{[True outcome (TO)]})&&=(1-\epsilon_{+})^{k_{+}}(1-\epsilon_{-})^{k_{-}},\\ &P(\hat{w}_{ij}=-y_{ij}\ \text{[Inverse outcome (IO)]})&&=\epsilon_{+}^{k_{+}}\epsilon_{-}^{k_{-}}.\\ \end{aligned}\right. (19)

We calculate Copeland scores from the matrix 𝐖\mathbf{W}:

SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dW​(i)=∑jN−1w^i​j,S^{W}_{Copeland}(i)=\sum_{j}^{N-1}\hat{w}_{ij}, (20)

and compute the probabilities of having the correct Copeland score P⁡(R∙,TO)P(R_{\bullet},\text{TO}):

P⁡(R1,TO)\displaystyle P(R_{1},\text{TO}) =(1−ϵ+)k+​(N−1)​(1−ϵ−)k−​(N−1),\displaystyle=(1-\epsilon_{+})^{k_{+}(N-1)}(1-\epsilon_{-})^{k_{-}(N-1)}, (21)

...\displaystyle...

This formulation separates ϵ+\epsilon_{+} and ϵ−\epsilon_{-} whenever k+≠k−k_{+}\neq k_{-}, and the two rates can be estimated accordingly. The behavior of d​P​(Rm,TO)/d​NdP(R_{m},\text{TO})/dN here at 𝐖\mathbf{W} is similar to that of at 𝐙\mathbf{Z}; both 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐙\mathbf{Z} are antisymmetric.

Estimation of error

The SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZ/WS^{Z/W}_{Copeland} scores computed from the observed 𝐙\mathbf{Z} or 𝐖\mathbf{W} matrix do not follow the perfect sequence N−1N-1, N−3N-3, N−5N-5, …, 5−N5-N, 3−N3-N, 1−N1-N due to the error in the output. We calculate its deviation from the perfect sequence, defined as the sum of the distances between elements in the two (ordered) sequences, denoted as ΔS\Delta_{S}. ΔS\Delta_{S} reveals the loss of scalability at pairwise comparison: ΔS\Delta_{S} grows as NN increases, at a speed inferior to the case of an all-zero 𝐙\mathbf{Z} matrix, in which case there is the closed form ΔS=N⁡(N+1)/2\Delta_{S}=N(N+1)/2.

The ΔS−N\Delta_{S}-N plot helps yield the estimates for ϵ/ϵ+,−\epsilon/\epsilon_{+,-}. For uniform error, at a specific value of ϵ\epsilon, (3) realizes a set of probabilities for elements in 𝐙\mathbf{Z} to take values of -1, 0, 1, respectively; the resulting 𝐙\mathbf{Z} matrix helps compute the ΔS\Delta_{S} at this ϵ\epsilon level. The error-free case (ϵ=0\epsilon=0) reproduces the perfect sequence (ΔS=0\Delta_{S}=0); as ϵ\epsilon increases, elements in 𝐙\mathbf{Z} get more random, and the deviation ΔS\Delta_{S} increases. Computing for different NN and fitting the ΔS−N\Delta_{S}-N plot from the measured 𝐙\mathbf{Z} to plots from ϵ\epsilon-specific 𝐙\mathbf{Z}s reveals the best-fit error level.

For positional bias, similarly, a set of ϵ+,ϵ−\epsilon_{+},\epsilon_{-} results in a simulated ΔS−N\Delta_{S}-N curve calculated from 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The ground-truth 𝐖\mathbf{W} is computed from the LLM output, and the best-fit ϵ+,ϵ−\epsilon_{+},\epsilon_{-} can be estimated accordingly. In practice, a subset of observations from the repeated comparisons can be used to cross-validate the error estimates: consider k+s≤k+k_{+}^{s}\leq k_{+} and k−s≤k−k_{-}^{s}\leq k_{-}, and use the corresponding 𝐖k+s,k−s\mathbf{W}^{k_{+}^{s},k_{-}^{s}} to obtain the estimates ϵ+k+s,k−s,ϵ−k+s,k−s\epsilon_{+}^{k_{+}^{s},k_{-}^{s}},\epsilon_{-}^{k_{+}^{s},k_{-}^{s}}; check the consistency of estimates across the values of k+s,k−sk_{+}^{s},k_{-}^{s} and report the average results.

The Bradley-Terry model

The Bradley-Terry (BT) model (Bradley and Terry, 1952) is widely used for efficiently constructing a ranking over objects from their pairwise comparison (Huang et al., 2006; Menke and Martinez, 2008; Turner and Firth, 2012, e.g.,). It is adopted by (Liusie et al., 2024) to turn the LLM preferences into an effective ranking using a subset of the comparison outcomes. The model assumes relative scores for the compared objects and constructs a maximum likelihood estimator to yield the optimal scores that meet the comparison outcomes, which can be solved with Zermelo’s algorithm (Zermelo, 1929) and notably its recent faster variant (Newman, 2023).

Assume a set of scores for the NN objects, s1,s2,…,sNs_{1},s_{2},...,s_{N}. For the original (unbiased) BT model, the probability of ii better than jj depends on the scores of ii and jj via the sigmoid function σ⁡(x)=1/(1+e−x)\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}): P⁡(i​ better than ​j)=σ⁡(si−sj)=esi/(esi+esj)=πi/(πi+πj)P(i\text{ better than }j)=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})=e^{s_{i}}/(e^{s_{i}}+e^{s_{j}})=\pi_{i}/(\pi_{i}+\pi_{j}), writing esie^{s_{i}} as πi\pi_{i} (following (Newman, 2023)). The probability of observing y^i​j∈[0,1]\hat{y}_{ij}\in[0,1] is then P⁡(y^i​j)=σ​(si−sj)y^i​j​[1−σ⁡(si−sj)]1−y^i​j=[πi/(πi+πj)]y^i​j​[πj/(πi+πj)]1−y^i​jP(\hat{y}_{ij})=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})^{\hat{y}_{ij}}[1-\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})]^{1-\hat{y}_{ij}}=[\pi_{i}/(\pi_{i}+\pi_{j})]^{\hat{y}_{ij}}[\pi_{j}/(\pi_{i}+\pi_{j})]^{1-\hat{y}_{ij}}. Best-fit scores s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N} are estimated from maximizing the complete likelihood of observing all the outcomes y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij}, i.e., s^1:N=argmaxs1:NΠi,jP(y^i​j)\hat{s}_{1:N}=argmax_{s_{1:N}}\Pi_{i,j}P(\hat{y}_{ij}).

Consider the error in the LLM output and incorporate bias into the BT model. The idea is adding a bias shift, following (Liusie et al., 2024): (si−sj)→(si−sj−ϵ)(s_{i}-s_{j})\rightarrow(s_{i}-s_{j}-\epsilon). In this case,

P†​(i​ better than ​j,ϵ)=σ⁡(si−sj−ϵ)=esiesi+eϵ​esj=πiπi+eϵ​πj.P_{\dagger}(i\text{ better than }j,\ \epsilon)=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j}-\epsilon)=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{e^{s_{i}}+e^{\epsilon}e^{s_{j}}}=\frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}}. (22)

Best-fit s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N} are estimated with

s^1:N=argmaxs1:NΠi,jP†(y^i​j,ϵ).\hat{s}_{1:N}=argmax_{s_{1:N}}\Pi_{i,j}P_{\dagger}(\hat{y}_{ij},\epsilon). (23)

See Supplementary Materials E for the iteration procedure of the biased BT model. An alternative idea is adding a multiplicative term to the sigmoid, P⁡(x)=σ⁡[(1−ϵ)​x]P(x)=\sigma[(1-\epsilon)x]; yet this formulation is not effective as we consider the ranking of the objects instead of their absolute scores. The BT model applies to repeated comparisons between object pairs; the strength matrix (Newman, 2023) 𝐗={x^i​j}\mathbf{X}=\{\hat{x}_{ij}\} where x^i​j\hat{x}_{ij} is the count of ii beating jj.

We can use this biased BT model to estimate the error rate ϵ\epsilon by adding constraints to the estimated scores. For example, we can assume the obtained s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N} to have a small/large spread and then search for the optimal ϵ\epsilon that minimizes/maximizes the spread of s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N}. Moreover, with a given ϵ\epsilon, e.g., estimated from our model, we can obtain the scores s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N} and the corresponding text ranking.

Materials

Text materials. Five types of text input are used in the experiment (Table 1; see sample texts in Supplementary Materials A): (i) pseudo-word paragraphs, (ii) pseudo paragraphs, (iii) advertising slogans, (iv) short poems, (v) academic abstracts. For (i), we generate 100 paragraphs of pseudo-word (void of meaning) sentences. For (ii), we generate 100 paragraphs with random English words. For (iii), we consider 100 popular commercial slogans (with one-line introductions) 11 1 https://advertisingnews.com/popular-slogans/. For (iv), we consider 100 famous short poems on PoetrySoup22 2 https://www.poetrysoup.com/famous/poems/short/top_100_famous_short_poems.aspx. For (v), we consider 100 abstracts of articles (across disciplines) published on Science Advances in May 2025. The five types of text have different average numbers of words and average numbers of tokens (converted from the text string) when fed into the LLM.

LLMs. We adopt six popular LLMs: ChatGPT (4.1 mini), Claude (3.5 sonnet), Deepseek (V3-30324), Gemini (2.5 Flash), Grok (3 mini), and Qwen (2.5-72B). The stochastic level (temperature) is set uniformly at 0.1. The following zero-short prompt is used: (system) You are a senior [text type] evaluation expert with rich experience in literary appreciation and judgment. Please conduct comprehensive text evaluations based on quality, creativity, expression effectiveness, and other dimensions. Only respond with 1 or 2; no explanation needed. (user) Compare the following two [text type] and indicate which one is better. Output only the number: 1 if Text 1 is better, 2 if Text 2 is better. Text 1: {\{text}\}. Text 2: {\{text}\}. Three prompt variants are considered in the robustness checks (Supplementary Materials B).

Results

Scalability of text ranking based on pairwise comparisons. We visualize the probability of the #​m\#m-ranking text obtaining the correct Copeland score, P⁡(Rm,T​O)P(R_{m},TO), constructed from LLMs’ pairwise preferences. Show the results for m=1m=1 to 8. For uniform error, the scores SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZS_{Copeland}^{Z} are calculated on matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z}; simulations verify that d​P​(Rm,TO)/d​N<0dP(R_{m},\text{TO})/dN<0 for different ϵ\epsilon and mm (Figure 1(a); ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1 to 0.5). P⁡(R∙,T​O)P(R_{\bullet},TO) approaches P⁡(R1,T​O)P(R_{1},TO) when ϵ\epsilon is small, as the terms with the multipliers of ϵ\epsilon vanish (see equation (8)); the P⁡(R2−8,T​O)−NP(R_{2-8},TO)-N curves thus overlap the P⁡(R1,T​O)−NP(R_{1},TO)-N curve. The difference between P⁡(R1,T​O)P(R_{1},TO), P⁡(R2,T​O)P(R_{2},TO), and P⁡(R3,T​O)P(R_{3},TO) can be seen, for example, at a large ϵ=0.5\epsilon=0.5 (Figure 1(a) inset).

For repeated comparisons, SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dWS^{W}_{Copeland} are calculated on 𝐖\mathbf{W}, and P⁡(R∙,T​O)P(R_{\bullet},TO) are dependent on the counts of comparisons k+k_{+}, k−k_{-} as well as the error rates ϵ+\epsilon_{+}, ϵ−\epsilon_{-}. Similar to uniform error, d​P​(Rm,TO)/d​N<0dP(R_{m},\text{TO})/dN<0 for different mm and combinations of k+k_{+}, k−k_{-}, ϵ+\epsilon_{+}, ϵ−\epsilon_{-} (Figure 1(b1)-(b4); four sets of parameter values are shown). Consistently, switching the values of k+/−k_{+/-} and ϵ+/−\epsilon_{+/-} simultaneously retains the outcome (Figure 1(b3)-(b4)) due to the interchangeable role of these two sets of parameters in indicating the positional bias. Overall, simulation results confirm that for sufficiently large NN, d​P​(Rm,TO)/d​N<0dP(R_{m},\text{TO})/dN<0 for any mm and error rates ϵ/ϵ+,−\epsilon/\epsilon_{+,-}: the Copeland ranking constructed from the observation matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z} or 𝐖\mathbf{W} are NOT scalable, i.e., the ranking gets more error-prone when more objects are compared.

Estimation of LLMs’ error at text comparison. We demonstrate the estimation with short poems as the input text and ChatGPT as the LLM, first at uniform error ϵ\epsilon, i.e., conducting two comparisons between each text pair with either text placed in the front and combining the two preferences. The observation matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is constructed from the preferences y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} and the Copeland scores SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZS_{Copeland}^{Z} are calculated on 𝐙\mathbf{Z} (Figure 2a, b). We sample nn texts from the ensemble, calculate the SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZS_{Copeland}^{Z} on the corresponding sub-matrix of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}, and sum the difference between the obtained and the perfect Copeland score sequence, ΔS\Delta_{S}. For each 2≤n≤N2\leq n\leq N, we conduct 200 runs of the sampling and compute the mean ΔS\Delta_{S}. We fit the empirical ΔS,o​b​s−N\Delta_{S,obs}-N curve to the ΔS,ϵ−N\Delta_{S,\epsilon}-N curves (Figure 2c) calculated with synthetic 𝐙\mathbf{Z} generated at different levels of ϵ∈[0,0.5]\epsilon\in[0,0.5], using grid search at interval 0.005. Each ΔS,ϵ\Delta_{S,\epsilon} averages over 10 synthetic 𝐙\mathbf{Z} at a certain ϵ\epsilon.

We collect the outcomes of three runs of comparison and conduct the estimation three times; one instance of the matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and the calculated Copeland scores SC​o​p​e​l​a​n​dZS_{Copeland}^{Z} is illustrated (Figure 2a, b). Fitting the empirical ΔS,o​b​s−N\Delta_{S,obs}-N to synthetic ΔS−N\Delta_{S}-N curves (Figure 2c) reveals a clear best-fit ϵ=0.130\epsilon=0.130 with near-zero misfit (Figure 2c inset), i.e., a uniform error rate of 13.0%\%. The three instances of the outcome are almost identical, having the commutativity scores Sc​o​m=39.01%,38.95%,39.03%S_{com}=39.01\%,38.95\%,39.03\% and the same best-fit ϵ\epsilon.

We then demonstrate the estimation at positional bias with repeated comparisons. We consider a comparison order sequence K=[+,−,+,−,+,−]K=[+,-,+,-,+,-], reduced to k+/−=3k_{+/-}=3. We show the results at 𝐖1,1\mathbf{W}^{1,1} to 𝐖3,3\mathbf{W}^{3,3}; 𝐖1,1\mathbf{W}^{1,1} reduces to the 𝐙\mathbf{Z} at uniform error. We look for the best-fit ϵ+,ϵ−∈[0,0.5]\epsilon_{+},\epsilon_{-}\in[0,0.5] using 2-D grid search, minimizing the summed distance between the empirical ΔS,o​b​s−N\Delta_{S,obs}-N and the synthetic ΔS−N\Delta_{S}-N curves, as before.

Figure 3 shows the estimates of ϵ+,ϵ−\epsilon_{+},\epsilon_{-} at the nine cases 𝐖1,1\mathbf{W}^{1,1} to 𝐖3,3\mathbf{W}^{3,3} (left inset) and the average result (main heatmap), whose diagonal elements, corresponding to ϵ+=ϵ−=0:0.005:0.5\epsilon_{+}=\epsilon_{-}=0:0.005:0.5 (right inset), concur with the curve at uniform error (Figure 2 inset). Best-fit ϵ+=0.155,ϵ−=0.100\epsilon_{+}=0.155,\epsilon_{-}=0.100 on the average 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The best-fits slightly vary under different values of k+,k−k_{+},k_{-}. One possibility is that instances of the LLM’s output from a series of comparisons are not independent, which is assumed when we calculate the observing probabilities ((3) and (18)): for the error of the output, there might be another positional factor regarding its place (tt) in the comparison series (KK), i.e., ϵ=ϵ⁡(K,t)\epsilon=\epsilon(K,t). This could be studied with KK-specific 𝐖K\mathbf{W}^{K} in future works.

We conduct the above error estimation with five types of text input (pseudo-word paragraphs, pseudo paragraphs, advertising slogans, short poems, academic abstracts) at six LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Qwen), under matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z} (uniform error) or 𝐖\mathbf{W} (positional bias, averaging over k+,k−∈[1,3]k_{+},k_{-}\in[1,3]).

Results are shown in Figure 4 (see Table S1 in the Supplementary Materials for values). Across the six LLMs, at pseudo-word paragraphs and pseudo paragraphs, the estimated ϵ,ϵ+/−\epsilon,\epsilon_{+/-} fall in [0.2, 0.5], while at slogans, poems, and abstracts, the estimates fall in [0, 0.2] (except for at slogans and abstracts under Gemini). This is consistent with the idea that LLMs are more error-prone when used to compare meaningless content, where a clear winner cannot be identified, than when used to compare meaningful content. At pseudo-word paragraphs and pseudo paragraphs, Qwen, Gemini, and Claude have the average error closer to 0.5, which is desirable, than Grok, DeepSeek, and ChatGPT. At the other text types, the average error is smaller at Qwen, Grok, and Claude than at ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini. Overall, in this experiment, Qwen obtained the best performance among the six LLMs, followed by Claude, Grok, then ChatGPT and DeepSeek; Gemini exhibited the worst performance. In most cases, the estimates of ϵ+/−\epsilon_{+/-} are not far from the estimate of ϵ\epsilon, especially at the three meaningful text types. There, the deviation of ϵ+/−\epsilon_{+/-} from uniform ϵ\epsilon is the largest under Gemini, followed by ChatGPT; the deviation is trivial at the other four LLMs.

We test three ideas to vary the baseline prompt (Supplementary Materials B): (V1) the text type is not specified; (V2) the prompt is presented in another language (Chinese); (V3) the system prompt is exempted. The variations of Sc​o​mS_{com} and ϵ\epsilon are summarized in Table 2 (see Table S2 in the Supplementary Materials for values). Overall, under these prompt variants where the original prompt is uniformly weakened in one way or another, Sc​o​mS_{com} and the estimated ϵ\epsilon increase, i.e., greater error rates are suggested. This is consistent with the finding that LLMs’ performance differs across languages (Lai et al., 2023) and levels of specificity (Murr et al., 2023). Of the six LLMs, Claude showed the highest robustness to the variation of prompts, followed by Gemini; interestingly, the error decreased at these two LLMs under certain prompt variants. Qwen demonstrated the least robustness, despite its good performance in the main result (Figure 4). In general, it is fair to note that the error estimates in this experiment are not sufficiently robust to the variation of prompts. Considering both the error rates and the robustness to prompts, Claude outperformed the other LLMs.

Our estimates of ϵ\epsilon align with the commutativity scores (Figure 6a): when Sc​o​mS_{com} is small/large, the estimated ϵ\epsilon is small/large, albeit the lack of strict monotonicity. Interestingly, the ratio of Sc​o​m/ϵS_{com}/\epsilon increases as ϵ\epsilon decreases: at pseudo-word paragraphs and pseudo paragraphs (as well as two other cases under Gemini) where ϵ>0.2\epsilon>0.2, Sc​o​m/ϵ<2.5S_{com}/\epsilon<2.5, while Sc​o​m/ϵ>2.9S_{com}/\epsilon>2.9 when ϵ<0.2\epsilon<0.2. This suggests that our estimates reflect the error of LLMs better than the commutativity scores.

Estimation with the biased Bradley-Terry model. We use the biased BT model to estimate ϵ\epsilon. Unlike at the unbiased model (Newman, 2023), at biased BT, the iterations of scores do not guarantee convergence (Supplementary Materials D); the scores increase synchronously, but the ranking stays invariant after a few iterations. We thus set the stopping criterion as no change in the ranking. For different values of ϵ\epsilon, the ranking is fixed after a handful of iterations (Figure 5a). We search for the ϵ∈[0,0.5]\epsilon\in[0,0.5] (grid interval 0.005) that minimizes or maximizes the spread of the obtained s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N}, m​a​x​(s^)−m​i​n​(s^)max(\hat{s})-min(\hat{s}). At one particular random seed for the initial scores s^1:N0\hat{s}_{1:N}^{0}, an optimal ϵo​p​t\epsilon_{opt} can be estimated (Figure 5b). We consider 200 random seeds for the initial scores (see corresponding ϵ\epsilon-spread plots at Supplementary Materials E) and calculate the frequency of ϵo​p​t\epsilon_{opt}. For example, with short poems under ChatGPT, the most frequent ϵo​p​t\epsilon_{opt} is in [0.24, 0.26] (Figure 5b inset).

We conduct such estimation with the biased BT model at different text types and LLMs. We report results minimizing or maximizing the spread of s^\hat{s} at k+/−=3/2k_{+/-}=3/2, 2/3, and 3/3, specified in the strength matrix 𝐗k+,k−\mathbf{X}^{k_{+},k_{-}} (Figure 6b; see Table S3 in the Supplementary Materials for values). Results show that in many cases the biased BT model yields the ϵo​p​t\epsilon_{opt} at the edge bins [0, 0.02] or [0.48, 0.50]. When 0.02<ϵo​p​t<0.480.02<\epsilon_{opt}<0.48, more coherent estimates are obtained at maximizing the score spread (lower panel of Figure 6b). In general, error estimates from the biased BT model are larger than those from our model, across LLMs and text types.

We can also adopt the uniform error ϵ\epsilon estimated from our model to calculate the scores s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N} from the biased BT model to construct a ranking over the compared texts. For example, we consider advertising slogans as the input texts and the 100 slogans are ranked accordingly (see Supplementary Materials F). Rankings from different LLMs (with distinct ϵ\epsilon estimates) are correlated to a certain extent: the two largest correlations (measured by Spearman’s ρ\rho) are between Claude/Gemini (ρ=0.34\rho=0.34) and DeepSeek/Grok (ρ=0.30\rho=0.30).

Discussions

We utilize pairwise comparison to characterize LLMs’ output error without the need of ground truth. Our methodological contributions are three-fold: (1) we show the increasing error and thus the poor scalability of constructing a (Copeland) ranking of the objects from LLMs’ pairwise preferences; (2) considering either uniform or binary errors (i.e., positional bias), our model helps yield consistent estimates of LLMs’ error rates, which align with while surpassing the commutativity scores that count the proportion of erroneous preferences; (3) our model outperforms the biased Bradley-Terry model in delivering coherent estimates of LLMs’ error. Empirically, among the six LLMs, Claude stood out in this experiment. It is nonetheless indiscreet to overstate its performance edge here, as the error estimates were not robust enough to the variation of prompts. Extensive tests with different scales of comparison, different testing environments, different types of text (or non-text) input, detailed prompt engineering, and potentially auxiliary ground truth, facilitate the thorough assessment of a particular LLM at this task.

Besides empirical tests, this study opens avenues for future work. First, we can allow the LLM to give no preference (output 0); the zero-preference option can be incorporated into the model. This might help further study the binary positional bias, which are not significantly separated in the current results. Second, for repeated comparisons, we assume that the comparison order sequence does not play a role and the sequence breaks down to the counts k+k_{+}/k−k_{-}. We can drop this assumption and look into different sequences with KK-specific 𝐖K\mathbf{W}^{K}. Third, we use zero-shot prompts without reasoning; soliciting reasoning or showing examples (Zeng et al., 2024) may help reduce LLMs’ error. Updated versions of brand LLMs may or may not demonstrate a smaller error rate at this task. Last, as suggested in (Newman, 2023), the Bradley-Terry model can be solved alternatively with maximum a posteriori estimation by considering appropriate priors for the scores s^1:N\hat{s}_{1:N}; this can be investigated in future attempts.

Reliably quantifying the error in LLMs’ output precedes the mitigation of their error, which welcomes extensive exploration on effective strategies, such as inviting human annotation (Wang et al., 2023) or adopting retrieval-augmented generation techniques (Gao et al., 2023; Gai et al., 2024). Overall, studying the behavior of LLMs, in particular their limitations, is essential for controlling the actions of these artificial agents, reaping their benefits, and minimizing their harms (Rahwan et al., 2019), which answers the urgent call for promoting human-centered and responsible artificial intelligence (Yoo et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025). For us humans, the reliance on artificial agents that hallucinate simply because they do not understand (Mitchell, 2023), does not solidify itself, as it appears costless; the price can be high.

Academic abstracts. The Tijuana River, at the US-Mexico border, discharges millions of gallons of wastewater daily-sewage, industrial waste, and runoff-into the Pacific Ocean, making it the dominant source of coastal pollution in this region. This study examines how such wastewater influences coastal aerosols by tracking spatial gradients from near the border northward. Using benzoylecgonine (a nonvolatile cocaine metabolite) as a sewage tracer, we find that wastewater compounds-including a mixture of illicit drugs, drug metabolites, and chemicals from tires and personal care products-become aerosolized and are detectable in both water and air. Spatial analyses confirm that most measured chemicals concentrate in aerosols near the Tijuana River, potentially exposing local populations to tens of nanograms per hour (e.g., octinoxate and methamphetamine) via inhalation. This airborne pathway highlights a largely overlooked source of atmospheric pollution, emphasizing the need to reassess health risks in coastal regions as global water contamination continues to escalate. [153 words, 205 tokens]

Supplementary Materials B: Prompt variants

The following system prompt is applied: You are a senior [text type] evaluation expert with rich experience in literary appreciation and judgment. Please conduct comprehensive text evaluations based on quality, creativity, expression effectiveness, and other dimensions. Only respond with 1 or 2; no explanation needed.

The following variants of the baseline prompt are considered:

Variant 1 (ignoring the text type). Compare the following two texts and indicate the better one. Output only the number: 1 if Text 1 is better, 2 if Text 2 is better. Text 1: {\{text}\}. Text 2: {\{text}\}.

Variant 2 (changing the language).

比较以下两篇文本材料/广告语/短诗/文献摘要，指出哪一篇更优。仅输出数字：输出1如果文本1更好，输出2如果文本2更好。文本1: {\{text}\}. 文本2: {\{text}\}.[in Chinese]

Variant 3 (exempting the system prompt). Only the user prompt is used. Without the system prompt, in some runs, the LLM outputs no preference on Text 1 or 2, especially when comparing pseudo-word paragraphs or pseudo paragraphs. In these rare cases, we randomly assign 1 or 2.

Supplementary Materials D: Iterations for the biased BT model

For the original BT model, follow the notations and the fast iteration procedure in [25]:

P⁡(𝐗|π)=∏i​jP†​(i​ better than ​j,ϵ)x^i​j.P(\mathbf{X}|\pi)=\prod_{ij}P_{\dagger}(i\text{ better than }j,\ \epsilon)^{\hat{x}_{ij}}. (S1)

The log-likelihood is

l​o​g​P​(𝐗|π)=∑i​jx^i​j​l​o​g​P†​(i​ better than ​j,ϵ).log\ P(\mathbf{X}|\pi)=\sum_{ij}\hat{x}_{ij}log\ P_{\dagger}(i\text{ better than }j,\ \epsilon). (S2)

At the maximum likelihood estimator, differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to πi\pi_{i} and set it to zero:

d​[l​o​g​P​(𝐗|π)]/d​πi=0,πi=esi.\text{d}[log\ P(\mathbf{X}|\pi)]/\text{d}\pi_{i}=0,\ \ \pi_{i}=e^{s_{i}}. (S3)

The iteration equation for πi\pi_{i} can be obtained.

For the biased BT model, consider an additive shift, (si−sj)→(si−sj−ϵ)(s_{i}-s_{j})\rightarrow(s_{i}-s_{j}-\epsilon). In this case,

P†​(i​ better than ​j,ϵ)=σ⁡(si−sj−ϵ)=esiesi+eϵ​esj=πiπi+eϵ​πj.P_{\dagger}(i\text{ better than }j,\ \epsilon)=\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j}-\epsilon)=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{e^{s_{i}}+e^{\epsilon}e^{s_{j}}}=\frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}}. (S4)

There is

d​[l​o​g​P​(𝐗|π)]/d​πi=0⟹1πi​∑jx^i​j​eϵ​πjπi+eϵ​πj=∑jx^j​iπi+eϵ​πj,\text{d}[log\ P(\mathbf{X}|\pi)]/\text{d}\pi_{i}=0\Longrightarrow\frac{1}{\pi_{i}}\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ij}\frac{e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}}{\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}}=\sum_{j}\frac{\hat{x}_{ji}}{\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}}, (S5)

which yields the iteration

πi←∑jx^i​j​eϵ​πj/(πi+eϵ​πj)∑jx^j​i/(πi+eϵ​πj).\pi_{i}\leftarrow\frac{\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ij}e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j}/(\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j})}{\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ji}/(\pi_{i}+e^{\epsilon}\pi_{j})}. (S6)

Unlike the original BT model, here the iterations of π\pi do not guarantee convergence for non-zero ϵ\epsilon. For different ii, πi\pi_{i} increases synchronously due to the eϵe^{\epsilon} term in the numerator. Nonetheless, the ranking stays invariant after a few iterations, and we set the stopping criterion as no change in the ranking.

Alternatively, with a multiplicative bias P⁡(x)=σ⁡[(1−ϵ)​x]P(x)=\sigma[(1-\epsilon)x],

P‡​(i​ better than ​j,ϵ)=σ⁡[(1−ϵ)​(si−sj)]=(esi)ϵ−1(esi)ϵ−1+(esj)ϵ−1=πi′πi′+πj′,πi′=(esi)ϵ−1.P_{\ddagger}(i\text{ better than }j,\ \epsilon)=\sigma[(1-\epsilon)(s_{i}-s_{j})]=\frac{(e^{s_{i}})^{\epsilon-1}}{(e^{s_{i}})^{\epsilon-1}+(e^{s_{j}})^{\epsilon-1}}=\frac{\pi^{\prime}_{i}}{\pi^{\prime}_{i}+\pi^{\prime}_{j}},\ \ \pi^{\prime}_{i}=(e^{s_{i}})^{\epsilon-1}. (S7)

There is

d​[l​o​g​P​(𝐗|π′)]/d​πi′=0⟹1πi′​∑jx^i​j​πj′πi′+πj′=∑jx^j​iπi′+πj′,\text{d}[log\ P(\mathbf{X}|\pi^{\prime})]/\text{d}\pi_{i}^{\prime}=0\Longrightarrow\frac{1}{\pi_{i}^{\prime}}\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ij}\frac{\pi_{j}^{\prime}}{\pi_{i}^{\prime}+\pi_{j}^{\prime}}=\sum_{j}\frac{\hat{x}_{ji}}{\pi_{i}^{\prime}+\pi_{j}^{\prime}}, (S8)

which yields the iteration

πi′←∑jx^j​i​πj′/(πi′+πj′)∑jx^j​i/(πi′+πj′).\pi_{i}^{\prime}\leftarrow\frac{\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ji}\pi_{j}^{\prime}/(\pi_{i}^{\prime}+\pi_{j}^{\prime})}{\sum_{j}\hat{x}_{ji}/(\pi_{i}^{\prime}+\pi_{j}^{\prime})}. (S9)

When only considering the ranking of the compared objects, the absolute scores s1:Ns_{1:N} do not matter, and thus the multiplicative bias is not effective.

Another possible formulation of the biased BT model is:

P⁡(i​ better than ​j)=(1−ϵ)​σ​(si−sj)+ϵ⁡[1−σ⁡(si−sj)]=(1−ϵ)​πi+ϵ​πjπi+πj.P(i\text{ better than }j)=(1-\epsilon)\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})+\epsilon[1-\sigma(s_{i}-s_{j})]=\frac{(1-\epsilon)\pi_{i}+\epsilon\pi_{j}}{\pi_{i}+\pi_{j}}. (S10)

However, this formulation does not yield an effective iteration procedure for efficient optimization, as πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} are not separated in the numerator and the denominator.
